scope: Primary-source evidence for a hybrid RGB markerless + visible anatomical marker motion-capture presentation. All reported performance belongs to published studies, not the current project.
recommended_positioning_ko: 다중 RGB 카메라 기반 markerless pose estimation에 선택적 가시광 해부학적 표면 마커 관측을 결합하여, 분절 자세와 관절 운동학 추정의 정확도 및 강건성 향상을 검증한다.
research_question_ko: 동일한 RGB 영상과 보정 조건에서, sparse pose keypoints에 해부학적 표면 마커 관측을 추가하면 발·무릎 주변의 3차원 위치 및 분절 방향 추정이 개선되는가?
terminology_and_caveats: Use marker-assisted markerless motion capture, hybrid optical motion capture, visible-light anatomical marker tracking, or RGB-based hybrid motion capture; define hybrid explicitly because commercial systems also use this word.

Do not say all pose estimation models detect only joint centres or cannot detect anatomical landmarks. Keypoint definitions depend on the training dataset and model; dense biomechanical landmark models already exist.
Preferred claim: Sparse, general-purpose pose keypoints may insufficiently constrain segment axial rotation and task-specific anatomical coordinate systems.
An anatomical surface landmark, an estimated joint centre, and the centre of a visible sticker are different quantities. State the palpation/placement protocol and any geometric offsets explicitly.

A single point does not determine full 3D orientation. Two endpoints specify a segment axis but not rotation about that axis; additional non-collinear landmarks, constraints, or model cues are required.
Visible markers can add subject-specific anatomical observations. Improved accuracy is a hypothesis to test, not an established result of this project.

Skin-mounted stickers remain affected by soft-tissue artefact (STA), placement error, occlusion, illumination, and motion blur. Infrared marker-based comparison is a reference-system comparison, not direct bone-motion ground truth.
Use concurrent validity, agreement, systematic bias, limits of agreement, repeatability, and robustness. Correlation alone is insufficient to establish accuracy.

Qualisys Miqus is a family: M1/M3/M5 use infrared marker tracking; Miqus Video records RGB; Miqus Hybrid switches between RGB and marker modes. Verify the actual laboratory model before naming the benchmark.
Do not compare MAE, RMSE, and RMSD as if interchangeable, and do not pool study values across different tasks, cameras, joint definitions, or filtering conditions.

papers.citation: Uhlrich SD, Falisse A, Kidzinski L, et al. (2023). OpenCap: Human movement dynamics from smartphone videos. PLoS Computational Biology 19(10): e1011462.
papers.status: Peer-reviewed original study; open access CC BY
papers.conditions: 10 healthy adults; walking, squatting, sit-to-stand, drop jumps; two iPhones versus marker-based optical motion capture and force plates.
papers.results: Joint-angle MAE 4.5 degrees across 18 rotational degrees of freedom and activities; degree-of-freedom range 1.7-10.3 degrees. Predicted anatomical markers improved mean kinematic accuracy by 3.4 degrees relative to using video keypoints directly.
papers.slide_use: Accessible RGB/smartphone workflow is feasible. Sparse keypoints are commonly supplemented by anatomical marker prediction and biomechanical constraints.
papers.avoid: Do not label these values as project results. OpenCap predicts virtual anatomical markers; it does not observe the proposed colored physical stickers.

papers.citation: Kanko RM, Laende EK, Davis EM, Selbie WS, Deluzio KJ. (2021). Concurrent assessment of gait kinematics using marker-based and markerless motion capture. Journal of Biomechanics 127:110665.
papers.conditions: 30 healthy adults, treadmill walking; eight video cameras and seven infrared cameras; simultaneous recording.
papers.results: Joint-centre RMSD below 2.5 cm except hip (3.6 cm). Global segment-angle RMSD below 5.5 degrees except rotations about the long axis of a segment.
papers.slide_use: A balanced evidence example: markerless gait measurements can agree well while long-axis rotations remain challenging.
papers.avoid: Do not state that every joint angle has error below 5.5 degrees; the paper describes global segment angles and explicitly excludes long-axis rotations.

papers.citation: Needham L, Evans M, Cosker DP, et al. (2021). The accuracy of several pose estimation methods for 3D joint centre localisation. Scientific Reports 11:20673.
papers.conditions: 15 healthy adults; walking, running, countermovement jumps; synchronized nine-camera RGB system and 15-camera Qualisys Oqus system at 200 Hz; pretrained OpenPose, AlphaPose, DeepLabCut human models.
papers.results: Hip and knee joint-centre estimates showed systematic differences of approximately 30-50 mm. Ankle differences were 1-15 mm depending on activity. Authors suggested training-label semantics/errors as a likely contributor.
papers.slide_use: Dataset keypoint semantics and anatomical joint-centre definitions matter in addition to camera reconstruction accuracy.
papers.avoid: Results concern the tested older pretrained model versions; they do not establish the error of every contemporary pose model.

papers.citation: Wren TAL, Isakov P, Rethlefsen SA. (2023). Comparison of kinematics between Theia markerless and conventional marker-based gait analysis in clinical patients. Gait & Posture 104:9-14.
papers.conditions: 36 clinical gait patients aged 2-25 years; concurrent Theia3D and Vicon; subgroups included foot deformities (25), orthoses (9), and assisted gait (6).
papers.results: RMSD below 6 degrees except pelvic tilt, hip flexion, ankle inversion, foot progression, and transverse hip/knee/ankle rotations. After offset removal, all RMSD_offset below 6 degrees; subgroup RMSD_offset below 8 degrees.
papers.slide_use: Foot geometry, knee-axis identification, assistive devices, and model offsets warrant task-specific validation.
papers.avoid: Offset-corrected agreement is not the same as absolute angular accuracy.

papers.citation: Turner JA, Chaaban CR, Padua DA. (2024). Validation of OpenCap: A low-cost markerless motion capture system for lower-extremity kinematics during return-to-sport tasks. Journal of Biomechanics 171:112200.
papers.conditions: Athletes 12-18 months after ACL reconstruction; 437 trials of jump-landing-rebound, single-leg hop, lateral-vertical hop; two smartphones versus 10-camera marker-based system.
papers.results: Pooled MAE 3.85 degrees and RMSE 4.34 degrees. Sagittal hip/knee CMC above 0.94; ankle CMC 0.84-0.93. Frontal CMC 0.47-0.78 and transverse CMC 0.51-0.60.
papers.slide_use: Agreement depends on movement plane: sagittal flexion can appear strong while frontal/transverse waveform agreement is weaker.
papers.avoid: CMC is a waveform agreement measure, not a position error in millimetres. The preprint used different correlation terminology; cite final published CMC values.

papers.citation: Falisse A, Uhlrich SD, Chaudhari AS, Hicks JL, Delp SL. (2025). Marker Data Enhancement for Markerless Motion Capture. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 72(6):2013-2022.
papers.status: Peer-reviewed original study; CC BY 4.0 verified from full-text XML
papers.conditions: Marker enhancer trained from 1176 subjects and 1433 hours of synthesized keypoints/anatomical markers. Accuracy benchmark uses movement videos; generalizability evaluated separately with synthetic unseen movements.
papers.results: 20 video keypoints mapped to 43 anatomical markers. Accuracy-task rotational RMSE: LSTM mean 4.1 degrees (maximum degree-of-freedom error 8.7) versus direct video-keypoint use mean 9.6 (maximum 43.1).
papers.slide_use: Anatomical information beyond sparse pose keypoints can improve biomechanical estimates. Distinguish inferred anatomical markers from physically observed landmarks.
papers.avoid: Do not imply that adding visible stickers has already produced this improvement; this paper evaluates learned marker enhancement.

papers.citation: Ancillao A, Aertbelien E, De Schutter J. (2021). Effect of the soft tissue artifact on marker measurements and on the calculation of the helical axis of the knee during a gait cycle: A study on the CAMS-Knee data set. Human Movement Science 80:102866.
papers.conditions: Six adults with total knee arthroplasty, gait trials; concurrent fluoroscopy and optoelectronic thigh/shank marker measurements.
papers.results: Largest rigid STA effect at thigh approximately 10 degrees and 18 mm; shank during swing approximately 7 degrees and 17 mm. Results varied substantially between subjects.
papers.slide_use: Visible stickers and infrared skin markers both track skin-relative observations; neither directly removes soft-tissue artefact or establishes true bone kinematics.
papers.avoid: Do not apply these numerical maxima to healthy subjects or to the current system without measuring them.

papers.citation: Liang H, Grant CJ, Bolgarskaya Y, et al. (2026). Validity of using a smartphone-based markerless motion capture system for quantitative analysis of human dynamic movements. Sports Biomechanics. Published online 19 June 2026.
papers.conditions: 41 participants; eight dynamic tasks including walking, running, jumping, cutting; simultaneous OpenCap and marker-based capture.
papers.results: Sagittal RMSE 7.0-13.4 degrees with r 0.70-0.99; systematic flexion/dorsiflexion overestimation 5-15 degrees. Out-of-plane RMSE 3.5-16.6 degrees, normalized RMSE 29.0-136.3%, r -0.09 to 0.80.
papers.slide_use: Contemporary validation also reports task, plane, and translation-dependent limits; a small absolute out-of-plane error can be large relative to its motion range.
papers.avoid: Do not collapse these task-specific ranges into one accuracy claim, and do not directly compare their RMSE to another paper's MAE.

papers.citation: Shin S, Li S, Li Z, et al. (2026). DeepGaitLab: Accurate and Flexible Markerless Motion Tracking Powered by Synthetic Data. Research Square, 24 July 2026.
papers.status: Preprint, not peer reviewed; optional latest-research context; CC BY 4.0
papers.conditions: 80 participants across healthy and mobility-limited cohorts; benchmark subset: 23 adults performing walking and physical-therapy tasks with multi-camera reference.
papers.results: In the 23-participant two-camera benchmark: RMSD 4.2 +/- 0.6 degrees for DeepGaitLab versus 5.9 +/- 1.3 for OpenCap across tasks/lower-limb degrees of freedom. Pipeline directly detects dense landmarks, triangulates them, and applies OpenSim.
papers.slide_use: Avoid claiming anatomical landmark estimation or multi-view RGB biomechanics is new in itself. Project contribution should be direct visible-marker observations and a measured hybrid-versus-markerless comparison.
papers.avoid: Label clearly as preprint if shown; keep separate from peer-reviewed evidence.

source_verification.primary_sources: Journal publisher articles, PubMed abstracts of original papers, and original full-text XML from Europe PMC. Secondary reviews used only for discovery, not as the basis for reported quantitative results.

proposed_validation_own_design_not_publi: Compare A: identical-camera markerless baseline; B: visible marker reconstruction; C: hybrid fusion. Keep calibration, synchronization, filtering and evaluation windows consistent.

First quantify 2D marker localization error and missed/false detections, then 3D marker position agreement, then segment orientation and joint kinematics. Detection mAP alone does not establish biomechanical accuracy.
Report 3D Euclidean trajectory error in mm, per-axis bias, RMSE/MAE and Bland-Altman limits of agreement. Report angle errors per joint and plane rather than only a grand average.
Use held-out subjects or recording sessions, not adjacent-frame random splits; stratify foot/knee visibility, view angle, motion speed, lighting and self-occlusion.
Evaluate controlled ankle/foot and knee motions first, then walking, squat, step-down and turning. This sequence is a proposed validation progression unless existing local data prove completion.

Align RGB and infrared systems in a shared metric coordinate frame and synchronize capture times. If separate stickers and reflective spheres are used, quantify their physical centre offset or use a shared dual-visible target.

Choose marker sets in consultation with the intended biomechanical model: medial/lateral femoral epicondyles, malleoli, calcaneus and metatarsal landmarks are candidates, not evidence that the present project already labeled those exact landmarks.
